body: Pre-delivery Boeing aluminum jets often look strikingly green, while Airbus aluminum jets usually do not — an observation that is partly true but far from the whole picture. The green is a corrosion-protective primer applied to the aircraft structure before its final livery, which also helps subsequent coatings adhere. Aircraft go through three coating stages — structural primer, intermediate coating and final decorative topcoats — and what looks like a single coat of green paint is typically two layers: a peelable Temporary Protective Coating (TPC, known as "Spraylat") over a Corrosion-Inhibiting Primer, the true undercoat. Airbus, Embraer, ATR and COMAC use broadly comparable surface-protection coatings, although they are not quite the same.

Composite airframes are the exception. The Boeing 787's fuselage and wings are built from carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer, which does not suffer galvanic or atmospheric metal corrosion, so Dreamliners roll out white or light gray-beige, coated with conductive and UV-protective primer; the Airbus A350's tan-beige primer serves a similar function. By contrast, the Boeing 737's fuselage remains fundamentally an aluminum structure of 1960s design, now in its fourth, MAX, generation, and the 777X has new wings but a primarily aluminum fuselage. The 777X's fuselage therefore wears the signature glossy emerald-green TPC, while its composite wings get a white or light-gray UV-protective topcoat; early-built 777-9s stored outdoors for years awaiting certification have also carried a strippable green film.

Airbus primers are chromate-free. Airbus began introducing chromate-free exterior primers on the A380 in 2016, almost a decade after the Superjumbo entered service, and European Union REACH chemical rules are phasing out hexavalent chromium more aggressively than in the United States; in 2025 the European Chemicals Agency unveiled a proposal to restrict carcinogenic hexavalent chromium substances across the EU. Airbus primers typically appear tan, beige or pale yellow, and Airbus generally does not use Boeing's glossy peelable emerald-green Spraylat transport film, so its structural primer is directly visible. Airbus is also multinational, with four home countries — the United Kingdom, France, Germany and Spain — and a distributed manufacturing model: barrels, wings and tails are fabricated, anodized and primed at different sites and subsidiaries, each applying its own corrosion-inhibiting primer with slightly different chemistry, so the assembled aircraft shows a patchwork of mismatched greens, yellows and tans. Major contractors include GKN Aerospace (Fokker Aerostructures) in the UK and the Netherlands, Latecoere in France and Spirit AeroSystems.

The photographs themselves are taken at different stages. Boeing's green jets are usually pictured with the TPC still on, on railcars or parked at Renton and Everett; the 737 fuselages built in Wichita, Kansas, travel about 2,000 miles (3,200 km) by open railcar to Renton and Everett, a journey of around ten to 12 days carrying three to four fuselages at a time and up to six, mostly on BNSF Railway through Nebraska, Wyoming and Montana to Washington via Spokane. The green TPC protects the relatively thin aluminum skin, where even minor scratches and indentations can require inspection. Airbus jets are more often photographed when unloaded from a BelugaXL or rolling off the final assembly line, sometimes on first customer acceptance flights — a later stage, when the raw structural epoxy primer gives a flat, chalky, matte finish. Overcast skies in Washington versus warm Mediterranean sunlight in Toulouse, and a camera's auto white balance, can shift the colors further, so the familiar comparison is partly a mismatch of timing.
en.summary: New Boeing aluminum jets often roll out green while Airbus jets usually do not — a difference explained by peelable protective film and primer, the composite-airframe exception, chromate-free primer rules, and the different production stages at which each maker's aircraft are photographed.
en.title: Why new Boeing planes are green before delivery, but Airbus aircraft aren't

body: 交付前的新波音鋁合金客機常呈鮮綠色，空中巴士鋁合金客機卻多半不是綠色——這個觀察部分正確，但遠非全貌。綠色其實是防腐蝕底漆，塗在最終塗裝之前，也幫助後續塗層附著。飛機塗裝分三個階段：結構底漆、中間塗層、最終裝飾面漆；看似一層綠漆，實際是可剝離臨時保護膜（TPC／Spraylat）加上防腐蝕底漆的組合。空中巴士、巴西航空工業、ATR與中國商飛也使用大致類似的表面防護塗層，只是配方不盡相同。

複合材料機身是例外。波音787以碳纖維強化聚合物打造機身與機翼，不會像鋁合金那樣產生電化學或大氣金屬腐蝕，因此出廠時呈白色或淺灰／米色，塗的是導電／抗紫外線底漆；空中巴士A350的棕褐色底漆功能類似。相對地，波音737機身至今仍是鋁合金結構、1960年代設計，現已發展到第四代MAX；777X換了新機翼，機身仍以鋁合金為主。777X的鋁合金機身就塗上標誌性的亮綠色TPC，複合材料機翼則是白色或淺灰色抗紫外線面漆；早期建造的777-9因等待認證在戶外存放多年，也覆有可剝離綠色薄膜。

空中巴士的底漆不含鉻酸鹽。空中巴士2016年起在A380上導入無鉻酸鹽外層底漆，距離超級巨無霸投入服務已近十年；歐盟REACH法規淘汰致癌六價鉻的步調比美國更積極，2025年歐洲化學品管理局更提案限制六價鉻物質在歐盟的使用。空中巴士的底漆多呈棕褐、米色或淡黃色，且一般不使用波音那種亮綠色可剝離Spraylat運輸膜，結構底漆直接可見。此外空中巴士橫跨英、法、德、西四國，採分散式製造：機身筒段、機翼與尾翼在不同工廠陽極處理並上底漆，各廠配方化學成分略有差異，色調也不同，組裝後便呈現深淺不一的拼貼感；主要承包商包括英國與荷蘭的GKN Aerospace（Fokker Aerostructures）、法國的Latecoere與Spirit AeroSystems。

拍照時機也造成對比。波音737機身在堪薩斯州威奇托建造後，須以開放式鐵路平板車運送2,000英里（3,200公里）到倫頓與艾弗雷特，全程約10至12天，一次運送3至4具機身（最多6具），路線主要由BNSF鐵路營運，經內布拉斯加、懷俄明、蒙大拿州，經斯波坎抵達華盛頓州；綠色TPC保護相對較薄的鋁合金蒙皮，免受製造與運輸過程的環境損傷，輕微刮痕或凹陷都可能需要檢查。熟悉的綠色波音照片多拍攝於鐵路運輸途中或停放在倫頓／艾弗雷特廠區時，仍覆著TPC；空中巴士照片則多在白鯨XL卸貨或下線、甚至首次客戶驗收飛行時拍攝，屬於較後期的階段，呈現的是原始結構環氧底漆的平坦粉狀霧面；再加上華盛頓州多陰天、土魯斯陽光溫暖，相機自動白平衡也可能改變色調，兩者其實是不同階段的比較。
zh.summary: 新出廠的波音鋁合金客機常呈鮮綠色，空中巴士卻多半不是——差異來自可剝離保護膜與防腐底漆、複合材料機身的例外、無鉻酸鹽底漆的法規背景，以及兩家製造商拍照時所處的不同生產階段。
zh.title: 為什麼新出廠的波音客機是綠色的？從可剝離保護膜到複合材料機身的塗裝解說
